Darling
DAR-ling
noun
From the Saxon deorling, a little dear one — deore, dear, with the diminutive -ling. In the Authorized Version it renders the Hebrew yachid, meaning only one or solitary, the same word used of Isaac as Abraham’s only son.

Biblical Definition

Darling is a term of endearment in modern English and something quite different in the Psalms. It twice renders the Hebrew yachid, the only one, and in both places the psalmist uses it of his own soul: “Deliver my soul from the sword; my darling from the power of the dog” (Psa 22:20), and “rescue my soul from their destructions, my darling from the lions” (Psa 35:17). The parallelism is exact — my soul answers to my darling — and the sense is not sentimental but arithmetical: the soul is a man’s only one. He has one body and may lose parts of it; he has one life and one soul, and there is no second. That is why the plea is so urgent and why our Lord’s question lands where it does: what shall a man give in exchange for his soul? There is nothing to exchange, because it is the only one he has. The setting of Psa 22 makes the word weightier still. This is the psalm that opens My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me, that describes pierced hands and feet and parted garments, and the very next verse cries “Save me from the lion’s mouth: for thou hast heard me” (Psa 22:21). The prayer for the yachid is on the lips of the only begotten Son.

Webster 1828 Definition

A dearly loved one; in the Psalms rendering the Hebrew for only one, used by the psalmist of his own soul as the single life he possesses.

DARLING, n. One much beloved; a favorite.

From the Saxon deorling, from deore, dear, with the diminutive termination -ling.

DARLING, adj. Dearly beloved; regarded with great affection.

In Psa 22:20 and 35:17 it renders the Hebrew yachid, only, solitary.

The same Hebrew is used of Isaac, Abraham’s only son (Gen 22:2).

Key Scripture

Psa 22:20 — "Deliver my soul from the sword; my darling from the power of the dog."

Psa 22:21 — "Save me from the lion's mouth: for thou hast heard me from the horns of the unicorns."

Psa 35:17 — "Lord, how long wilt thou look on? rescue my soul from their destructions, my darling from the lions."

Gen 22:2 — "And he said, Take now thy son, thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest, and get thee into the land of Moriah; and offer him there for a burnt offering upon one of the mountains which I will tell thee of."

Modern Corruption

The soul is treated as one component of a person among many — a dimension to be balanced against career, body, and relationships — where Scripture calls it the only one, with nothing to set beside it.

expand to see more

The corruption is the demotion of the soul to one item on a list. Modern speech divides a person into domains — physical, mental, emotional, financial, social, and somewhere among them the spiritual — and counsels balance among them, as though the soul were a sector requiring its due share of attention. The Hebrew behind darling refuses the arithmetic. Yachid means the only one. A man may lose his health and live, lose his money and live, lose his reputation and live; he has exactly one soul, and its loss is not a setback in one area but the end of him.

Recover the plain sense: our Lord put the whole matter into a question no one has answered — what shall a man give in exchange for his soul? The form of the question is the argument. An exchange requires something of comparable value to offer, and there is nothing, because whatever a man might offer belongs to the same short life he is trying to save. Then observe where the word sits in Psa 22. The psalm of the crucifixion, quoted by Christ from the cross, contains this prayer for the only one — and the same Hebrew describes Isaac bound on Moriah, the only son whom the father loved. Two only sons on two mountains, and on the second the ram did not appear.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Saxon deorling, a little dear one — rendering Hebrew yachid, the only one; the soul as a man’s single, unexchangeable life.

Darling — Saxon deorling, from deore, dear.

Renders the Hebrew yachid, only, solitary, an only child.

Set in parallel with my soul in both Psa 22:20 and Psa 35:17.

The same Hebrew describes Isaac, Abraham’s only son (Gen 22:2).

Psa 22 is the psalm of the crucifixion, quoted by Christ from the cross.

Usage

"The sense is not sentimental but arithmetical — the soul is the only one."

"What shall a man give in exchange for his soul? — there is nothing to offer."

"Two only sons on two mountains; on Calvary no ram was provided."
